title: Database-per-Service
subtitle: Enforcing strict data encapsulation, eliminating shared-schema coupling, and handling cross-service joins.
keyTakeaways: Database-per-Service mandates that each microservice exclusively owns its persistent storage; other services must interact via APIs, never direct database queries.
Shared databases destroy microservice autonomy: schema migrations in one service break adjacent services, and connection pool exhaustion cascades across the entire company.
Executing queries across decoupled databases is achieved via API Composition at the gateway or Event-Driven CQRS read projections.
architectureDiagram:
SHARED DATABASE ANTIPATTERN VS DATABASE-PER-SERVICE
SHARED DATABASE (Anti-Pattern: Tight Coupling & Blast Radius):
[ Order Service ] ------+
                        +---> [ Shared PostgreSQL Database ] (Single Point of Failure!)
[ Inventory Svc ] ------+

DATABASE-PER-SERVICE (Autonomous & Encapsulated):
[ Order Service ]      [ Inventory Service ]      [ Billing Service ]
       |                        |                         |
       v                        v                         v
[ Order Postgres ]     [ Inventory DynamoDB ]     [ Billing Postgres ]
(Private storage; services interact purely via gRPC APIs and Kafka events!)

sections.heading: Why Shared Databases Destroy Microservice Autonomy
sections.body: The most common architectural failure when migrating from a monolith to microservices is spinning up separate service containers while keeping a single shared relational database underneath. Multiple services write and read directly from the same SQL tables.
bullets: Bypassing Business Invariants: If the Inventory Service updates the `orders` table directly, it bypasses the validation and state machine rules inside the Order Service.
Schema Lock-Step Deployments: Renaming a column in the shared database requires synchronizing deployments across four independent teams simultaneously.
Connection Pool Starvation: A slow reporting query executed by the Analytics Service consumes all database connections, crashing the critical Payment Service.

codeSnippet.title: API Composition Pattern for Cross-Service Data Aggregation

sections.heading: Executing Joins and Queries Across Private Databases
sections.body: Once databases are private, executing traditional SQL `JOIN` statements across tables owned by different services is impossible. Distributed architectures resolve cross-database queries through two proven patterns.
bullets: API Composition: An aggregator service or edge API Gateway calls each service's API in parallel and merges the JSON results in application memory. Ideal for simple dashboards.

CQRS with Change Data Capture (CDC): Services emit state change events to Kafka. A dedicated Query Service consumes events from multiple topics and populates a denormalized read model (Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL read replica), allowing sub-10ms single-table queries across combined domain data.

tradeOffs.pros: Complete service autonomy; teams choose the optimal database engine (Polyglot persistence); bounded fault blast radius.
tradeOffs.cons: Cross-service relational joins are eliminated; distributed transactions require Sagas; eventual consistency across read models.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Production microservices in medium-to-large engineering organizations.

tradeOffs.pros: Native ACID cross-table JOINs and foreign key integrity; simple single-database backup operations.
tradeOffs.cons: Tight coupling between teams; schema changes risk breaking adjacent services; shared database is a single point of failure.

interviewTip: Defend Database-per-Service decisively: 'Microservices that share a database are a distributed monolith. To ensure true service autonomy, each microservice must own its private database. For queries requiring cross-service data, we use asynchronous event streaming to build a denormalized CQRS read model, completely avoiding direct database access across service boundaries.'
